title: Keva and Kavanah: A Rule of Life
hookLine: the last stretch is about living it: a short daily rule you choose yourself
carry: keva keeps the time, kavanah keeps the heart
tomorrow: what are the first words before your feet touch the floor?

lines: SHOULD A SPIRITUAL LIFE HAVE RULES?
cards: A notes-app list titled this year, with a goal for every part of life. A few weeks later it's a list of things you aren't doing.
So the last stretch of this path tries something smaller: a rule of three lines, chosen by you. One thing in the morning, one in the day, one at night. Short enough to keep on a bad Tuesday.
But can a rule that small hold a whole life? And should a spiritual life have rules at all? Jewish tradition has argued about exactly that.

teach.b: Here are both sides, each in its own voice. The first is Shammai, in Pirkei Avot: make your Torah study keva, fixed. A set time, every day, whether you feel like it or not.

The case for it is simple. Feelings come and go; a fixed time is still there on the day the feeling isn't. A rule carries you through the gray weeks, and often the feeling comes back while you're keeping it.

teach.h: RABBI SHIMON: DON'T LET IT GO ROTE.
teach.b: The second is Rabbi Shimon, also in Pirkei Avot: when you pray, don't make your prayer keva. Don't let it go rote, the same words rattled off like a grocery list.
Make it a real plea, said with kavanah, intention, meaning it. The case for that is just as strong. A rule kept on autopilot can turn into the thing itself, and the heart quietly leaves the room.
The Talmud even asks what keva means, and gives more than one answer: anyone whose prayer feels like a burden; anyone who doesn't say it as a plea; anyone who can't add anything new to it.
Notice that the two aren't really enemies.

teach.h: A TIME, AND A HEART INSIDE IT.
teach.b: Shammai is talking about protecting a time; Rabbi Shimon is talking about protecting the heart inside it.
The tradition keeps both: the siddur gives fixed words at fixed times, and the sages keep asking whether you meant them.
So a rule of three lines can hold a life, if you keep it fixed and keep asking.

how: Jewish life is built on fixed times, morning, afternoon and evening prayers, Shabbat each week, alongside the teaching that prayer needs kavanah, intention; some people keep a set time to study each day.

games.q: what does “a rule of three lines” mean?
o: a three-line poem written for the end of the year
the three daily prayer services in a synagogue
a short daily rule you choose: morning, day and night

games.q: fixed or felt — tap the pairs.
p: don't let your prayer go rote

s: Jewish tradition says rules always kill the feeling
Shammai says fix a time; Rabbi Shimon warns against going rote. the tradition keeps both.
the Talmud gives more than one answer to what 'fixed' prayer means
a burden, not a plea, or nothing new added: Berakhot lists several views.
a good rule of life should be long and detailed
three lines, small enough to keep on a bad week, fixed and still meant.

games.q: you love having a fixed prayer time. now state Rabbi Shimon's side at its strongest.
o: a fixed habit can quietly empty out, until you're saying words without meaning them.
fixed times are for beginners; experts only pray when they feel inspired.
rules are fine for study but never belong anywhere near prayer at all.
games.why: Rabbi Shimon's worry is rote: words rattled off like a list. he doesn't throw out the fixed prayers; he guards the heart inside them.

practice: Write your rule now, three lines only. One small thing for the morning, one for the day, one for the night, each something you could keep on your worst week.
Under it, write the one thing most likely to break it, and what you'll do when that happens.

wordCard.voice: A rule of three lines: your own short rule for each day, fixed like Shammai's study, and kept alive with Rabbi Shimon's kavanah.

orig.note: Hebrew: fixed, set. Shammai: make your Torah keva; Rabbi Shimon: don't make your prayer keva.

carryVoice: Your line: keva keeps the time, kavanah keeps the heart. Fixed enough to keep, alive enough to mean. The new stretch, begun.

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (Shammai: make your Torah study fixed)
Pirkei Avot 2:13 (Rabbi Shimon: do not make your prayer fixed, but a plea for mercy)
Berakhot 29b (what is 'fixed' prayer: a burden; not said as a plea; nothing new added)
